prompt:
You are writing for a decision-aid system used by government officials in
Odisha's Department of Panchayati Raj & Drinking Water. The system
automatically analyses village-level planning and spending records --
development plans, sanctions, payments, works and photo evidence from
Gram Panchayats, blocks, and districts -- and surfaces patterns worth an official's attention.

Your readers are busy block-, district- and state-level officials, not data
analysts. They read these insights to decide where to direct attention:
which districts to question, which records to reconcile, which local
practices to check at the next review.

Below are 15 findings from the analysis engine, each written in the engine's
internal style -- accurate but full of database language -- along with
reference figures for each. Rewrite each finding as an insight a senior
officer would find clear and actionable:
- a one-to-two-sentence lead the officer sees first;
- a short detail paragraph explaining what was found, which places are
  exceptions and in what way, and what is worth checking or asking at the
  next review.

Write naturally, in plain English. Use the reference figures where they
strengthen the point; use no number that is not provided. Be direct about
what the data can and cannot establish -- these records are incomplete in
known ways described below, and an insight that overstates certainty could
send an official after the wrong problem.

Background to reflect where relevant:
- Sanction records exist for only about one work in six, so figures on a
  sanctioned basis describe that subset, and a falling sanctioned value can
  mean fewer sanctions or fewer sanctions being entered.
- Cost-free activities (training, campaigns, services) began being recorded
  only in 2023-24, so activity counts jump at that boundary for a reporting
  reason, not a real one.
- Total cashbook spending has not grown across these years, while the share
  of spending linked to a planned activity rose from 2.7% to 53.2% -- a rise
  in "linked spending" is mostly better record-keeping.
- March concentrates payments every year; it is the fiscal year-end and this
  is normal government cash flow.
- Output categories "Code 101" to "Code 110" have no descriptions on file;
  nothing can be concluded about what they contain until the department
  supplies the decode.
- "Uncategorised" assets are works with no asset category recorded -- about
  two-thirds of all works; it is not itself a kind of asset.
- Only 17 works in the whole sample are marked completed, so completion
  figures measure recording practice, not delivery.
- Voucher and payment counts are workload, not a performance rating.
- This is a 20-Gram-Panchayat sample; percentages describe the sample, not
  the state.

Give your answer for all 15 findings, in order. Delimit each one exactly like this:

===FINDING 1===
LEAD: <the lead>
DETAIL: <the detail paragraph>
===FINDING 2===
LEAD: ...
DETAIL: ...

...and so on through ===FINDING 15===.

===FINDING 1===
LEAD: Spending remains below planned cost across almost every asset category, and the gap is spread across blocks rather than concentrated in one place.
DETAIL: Across the 5,630 costed activities, recorded spending was Rs 51.96 crore below planned cost. Rangeilunda had a gap of Rs 9.11 crore and spent Rs 2.73 crore of Rs 11.84 crore planned; Kalimela had a gap of Rs 5.90 crore and spent Rs 1.76 crore of Rs 7.65 crore planned. Banking Facilities showed no clear distribution pattern; reviews should focus on whether plans, expenditure links and work status are current, rather than treating this as an overspending issue.

===FINDING 2===
LEAD: Expenditure linked to planned activities rises over time whether viewed by month, quarter or fiscal year. This mainly indicates better linking of payment records, not growth in overall spending.
DETAIL: Total cashbook spending did not grow over these years, while the share linked to a planned activity rose from 2.7% to 53.2%. Officials should continue improving payment-to-activity reconciliation and avoid reading the trend as evidence of higher programme expenditure.

===FINDING 3===
LEAD: Recorded sanctioned value declines over time in five of the nine sampled districts, while Kandhamal moves in the opposite direction.
DETAIL: The declining pattern appears in Bargarh, Koraput, Cuttack, Sundargarh and Malkangiri; Khordha, Ganjam and Rayagada show no clear trend. Across the sample, annual recorded sanctions were Rs 6.13 crore in 2020-21 and Rs 3.57 crore in 2025-26, but sanction records exist for only about one activity in six, so districts should be asked whether the change reflects actual sanctions or incomplete entry.

===FINDING 4===
LEAD: On activities with sanctions recorded, the gap between expenditure and sanctioned amount is spread across districts in almost every asset category rather than being confined to one district.
DETAIL: The recorded gap totals Rs 5.02 crore; Ganjam accounts for Rs 1.68 crore, with Rs 4.61 crore spent against Rs 6.30 crore sanctioned, while Khordha spent Rs 3.33 crore against Rs 4.06 crore. Banking Facilities has no clear pattern. Because only about one activity in six has a sanction record, these are not programme-wide utilisation rates; reviews should first reconcile missing sanctions and expenditure links.

===FINDING 5===
LEAD: Codes 101 and 105 account for most recorded untied funds for public works in 19 of the 20 sampled Gram Panchayats, while Haldikudar follows a different pattern.
DETAIL: Code 101 carries Rs 34.88 crore, or 62.1% of the total, and Code 105 carries Rs 16.90 crore, or 30.1%. The department has no descriptions on file for Codes 101 to 110, so no conclusion can yet be drawn about what is being prioritised; obtain the code definitions and then check why Haldikudar differs.

===FINDING 6===
LEAD: Bhubaneswar block records the highest payment-processing workload in five of the six fiscal years; 2024-25 shows no clear leader.
DETAIL: Bhubaneswar accounts for 2,135 of the 8,529 vouchers in the sample, or 25.0%, compared with 945 in Rangeilunda and 885 in Bheden. Voucher counts indicate workload, not performance; reviews should check whether staffing and reconciliation arrangements are adequate for Bhubaneswar’s volume.

===FINDING 7===
LEAD: Missing asset classification is the largest public-works category in 19 of the 20 sampled Gram Panchayats; Govindapur is the only exception.
DETAIL: Of 9,418 public-work activities, 5,181, or 55.0%, are recorded as “Uncategorised,” meaning no asset category was entered. This does not describe a type of asset; Gram Panchayats should be asked to complete the classification field, while Govindapur’s different recording pattern may offer a practice worth examining.

===FINDING 8===
LEAD: Activities still marked “Activity Approved” account for Rs 41.61 crore of the gap between planned cost and recorded spending in 18 of the 20 sampled Gram Panchayats.
DETAIL: Only Rs 14.00 lakh is linked as spent against Rs 41.75 crore planned for this status, while ongoing works show Rs 24.76 crore spent against Rs 28.99 crore planned. Boipariguda and Laxmipur show no clear status pattern. Officials should check whether approved activities have not started, or whether payments and status updates are missing; “Buildings” also appears as a status value and should be corrected.

===FINDING 9===
LEAD: Payment volumes follow a recurring annual cycle at monthly and quarterly levels, with the usual concentration around the fiscal year-end. No clear pattern appears when totals are compared by fiscal year.
DETAIL: March-heavy payment processing is normal government cash flow and should not by itself trigger concern. Reviews should instead look for departures from the usual year-end pattern, delayed reconciliation or unusual backlogs in particular places.

===FINDING 10===
LEAD: Works marked “ongoing” hold 93.9% of the recorded general-fund amount for costed activities, and this pattern appears in 18 of the 20 sampled Gram Panchayats.
DETAIL: Ongoing works account for Rs 28.59 crore of Rs 30.43 crore, while abandoned works account for Rs 1.15 crore. Boipariguda and Laxmipur show no clear pattern. Reviews should test whether work statuses are being updated promptly and examine the funds attached to abandoned works rather than treating the concentration itself as evidence of poor delivery.

===FINDING 11===
LEAD: Expenditure linked to activities increases across quarters in six of the nine sampled districts, but Bargarh, Koraput and Cuttack follow different patterns.
DETAIL: The increasing pattern appears in Khordha, Ganjam, Kandhamal, Sundargarh, Malkangiri and Rayagada. Several of the highest totals occur in first quarters, including Rs 1.99 crore in 2026-Q1 and Rs 1.92 crore in 2025-Q1, consistent with normal March concentration. Because linked spending has risen mainly through better record-keeping, districts should explain differences in payment linking rather than assume underlying spending has increased.

===FINDING 12===
LEAD: Almost all expected beneficiaries are attached to activities still marked “Activity Approved,” suggesting that beneficiary and status records need reconciliation.
DETAIL: Approved activities carry 2,03,534 of the 2,06,929 expected beneficiaries in the sample, or 98.4%; ongoing works carry 2,759, while completed works record none. Boipariguda and Laxmipur show no clear pattern. These are expected beneficiaries, not people verified as reached, and only 17 works in the sample are marked completed, so officials should check status updates and beneficiary-field completion rather than infer delivery.

===FINDING 13===
LEAD: Half of the recorded untied funds for costed activities are mapped to “Theme 6 – Self-sufficient Infrastructure in Village,” which leads in 18 of the 20 sampled Gram Panchayats.
DETAIL: Theme 6 accounts for Rs 30.07 crore, or 50.4%, followed by Theme 4 – Water Sufficient Village at Rs 11.63 crore. Kalimela is the exception where Theme 4 leads; in Boipariguda, “Unmapped theme” leads. Reviews should ask Boipariguda to complete theme mapping and confirm that the concentration under Theme 6 reflects local plans rather than routine coding.

===FINDING 14===
LEAD: Among new works with sanction records, Code 101 accounts for almost the entire Rs 2.54 crore gap between sanctioned amount and expenditure; Chikilli shows no clear pattern.
DETAIL: Code 101 records Rs 14.94 crore spent against Rs 17.43 crore sanctioned, leaving a Rs 2.49 crore gap. This covers only the minority of activities with sanctions on file and cannot be treated as programme-wide utilisation. Because Codes 101 to 110 have no descriptions, obtain the decode before asking Gram Panchayats to explain the concentration, and check whether missing sanctions or expenditure links contribute to it.

===FINDING 15===
LEAD: All 6,893 photo uploads for new works are recorded under Code 101, even though that code represents only 32.8% of the activities in scope. This strongly warrants a check of evidence coding or system mapping.
DETAIL: Codes 102, 103, 109 and 110 record no photo uploads, while Chikilli shows no clear Gram-Panchayat-level pattern. As Codes 101 to 110 have no descriptions, the records cannot establish whether evidence is genuinely absent for other work types or has been assigned to a default code; obtain the code definitions and test the upload mapping before assessing compliance.
